lines.text: Romans wore their keys as rings.
A thin hoop held a tiny key set at right angles.

They opened small caskets that held jewelry and other valuables.

A worn key was harder to lose or to steal.
Most surviving ones are bronze or iron.

post.caption: Romans wore their keys as rings. A thin hoop held a tiny key set at right angles, and the keys really worked on locks for small boxes. They opened small caskets that held jewelry and other valuables. Roman clothes often lacked pockets, so a ring kept the key close, and a worn key was harder to lose or to steal. Most surviving ones are bronze or iron. Some are only about 2 centimeters across. Museums date them from the 1st to the 4th century AD. Harvard Art Museums and the Met both hold examples.
